label: Historical Fiction
description: Invented or embellished stories set against real history. Calibrated against Shakespeare in Love (Best Original Screenplay winner), Titanic, Gladiator, Braveheart, Saving Private Ryan, 1917, Inglourious Basterds and Amadeus.

criteria.name: Personal spine
criteria.description: The film is about one person's want and need, with history as the pressure on them, not the plot itself. You can say it in one sentence about a person, not an era.
criteria.weak: The story is a tour of the era; events happen and the lead reacts.
criteria.strong: A clear protagonist whose want (external) and need (internal) drive every act, established early and shown in action.

criteria.name: Fiction in the gaps
criteria.description: Invention goes where the historical record is silent (Shakespeare in Love invents Viola in Shakespeare's undocumented 1593). Real people stay consistent with the documented record; well-known facts are not contradicted without a clear dramatic reason.
criteria.weak: Contradicts well-documented events or turns real figures into something the record does not support, with no purpose.
criteria.strong: Invention sits in the gaps, real figures behave consistently with the record, and any deliberate license serves character or theme.

criteria.name: Dramatic irony
criteria.description: The known outcome, or a secret the audience holds, becomes a source of tension and poignancy rather than a spoiler (Titanic's sinking; Will confiding his love for Viola to Viola disguised as Thomas).
criteria.weak: The known outcome kills suspense, or the audience never knows more than the characters.
criteria.strong: The audience is deliberately given knowledge a character lacks, and scenes play on that gap.

criteria.name: Period antagonist
criteria.description: The opposition is the period's social forces (class, law, church, empire, money, war) embodied in a specific person with practical motives. Shakespeare in Love's Wessex embodies class, money, royal consent and male ownership in one scene.
criteria.weak: A generic villain whose evil is unmotivated, or no personified opposition at all.
criteria.strong: A specific antagonist with understandable, period-rooted reasons, through whom the era itself pushes back.

criteria.name: Theme with modern resonance
criteria.description: The story speaks to today without giving characters 21st-century values unexplained. Shakespeare in Love's art-versus-commerce theme recurs in nearly every scene.
criteria.weak: Preachy, absent, or carried by anachronistic speeches.
criteria.strong: A question that matters now, dramatized through period-true choices and repeated across scenes.

criteria.name: World texture
criteria.description: Period detail lives in action lines and behaviour (objects, work, manners), not lectures. Background is revealed through conflict, not explanation. Title cards are brief.
criteria.weak: Exposition dumps, encyclopedia tone, or characters explaining history to each other.
criteria.strong: Specific, lived-in detail shown on screen; backstory surfaces in arguments and choices.

criteria.name: Dialogue
criteria.description: Period flavour through rhythm and image rather than archaic vocabulary; modern clarity; distinct voices. Anachronistic winks are rationed (at most one per scene) and deliberate.
criteria.weak: Stilted thee-and-thou pastiche, or modern slang that breaks the period.
criteria.strong: Short, clear, speakable lines with a period cadence; each character sounds like themselves.

criteria.name: Convergence and ticking clocks
criteria.description: The private story and the historical event peak together, and dated deadlines create pressure ('two weeks from Saturday').
criteria.weak: The personal story and the history run in parallel without touching; no deadlines.
criteria.strong: Specific deadlines drive the middle, and the personal and historical climaxes collide.

criteria.name: Ending
criteria.description: History wins, but the character gets an emotional resolution. The ending is earned and true to the period (Viola leaves; the love survives as Twelfth Night).
criteria.weak: Rewrites history for comfort, or stops without emotional resolution.
criteria.strong: Bittersweet, earned, and faithful to what history allows.

criteria.name: Producibility
criteria.description: Period films are expensive (costume, crowds, ships, battles, locations). Scale is used sparingly and contained scenes carry the story.
criteria.weak: Large battles, crowds or sea scenes on most pages; the story only works at epic budget.
criteria.strong: A contained core (a few key locations) with spectacle saved for moments that matter.

bonus.name: Mirror device
bonus.description: A story-within-the-story (a rehearsal, trial, letter, ceremony, battle plan) echoes the main plot, as Shakespeare in Love's rehearsals of Romeo and Juliet mirror Will and Viola's romance.
bonus.weak: No inner story, or one that does not reflect the main plot.
bonus.strong: An inner story that comments on and propels the main story.

passFail.name: Industry format
passFail.description: Scene headings, action, character cues and dialogue in standard screenplay format.

passFail.name: Length
passFail.description: Roughly 90 to 120 pages for a feature.
